ECE 6390

Bit energy, symbol energy and noise

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how average signal power is distributed among information bits, coded bits and symbols.

An energy axis is useful only with its counting convention. Information bits describe the useful encoder input. Coded bits include redundancy. A modulation symbol labels m = log₂M coded bits. With code rate r = Rinfo/Rcoded, the rates satisfy Rcoded = Rinfo/r and Rs = Rinfo/(r m).

For average received carrier power C in watts, Eb, info = C/Rinfo, Eb, coded = C/Rcoded and Es = C/Rs, all in joules. Therefore Eb, coded = r Eb, info and Es = r m Eb, info. Changing r at fixed C and Rinfo preserves energy per information bit while changing the other energies and downstream rates.

Use N₀ as one-sided noise power density in W/Hz; a real noise process has two-sided density N₀/2. With equivalent noise bandwidth BN in hertz, N = N₀BN. Then Eb/N₀ = (C/N)BN/Rb and Es/N₀ = (C/N)BN/Rs. The bit rate Rb must match the chosen Eb. A full occupied RF width and a receiver equivalent noise bandwidth need not be numerically equal.

The adjustable figure holds received power and information rate fixed, varies coding and symbol labels, and separately computes in-band C/N using a declared noise bandwidth. Framing and pilots are excluded. A BER curve must use the same energy convention as the link calculation.

Example

At C = 1 W, Rinfo = 4 Mbit/s, rate 1/2 and QPSK, Rcoded = 8 Mbit/s and Rs = 4 Msym/s. Eb, info = Es = 0.25 µJ, while Eb, coded = 0.125 µJ. If BN = 2 MHz, Rinfo = 4 Mbit/s and C/N = 10 dB, Eb, info/N₀ = 10 × 2/4 = 5, or 6.99 dB.

Practice

1. At fixed received power and information rate, how do the two bit energies change when code rate drops from 1 to 1/2?

Apply C/R separately at the encoder input and output.

Information-bit energy stays unchanged. Coded rate doubles, so coded-bit energy halves. Bandwidth or symbol loading must accommodate that greater coded rate.

2. When does a quoted C/N equal Eb/N₀ numerically?

Keep the factor BN/Rb.

When the noise bandwidth BN equals the bit rate Rb under the declared conventions. The general relationship retains BN/Rb; equal units alone do not establish equality.
